opus-5.5.text:
Sure. The core idea behind EMMA is surprisingly simple, and I think that's part of what makes it interesting. We took a large multimodal foundation model, in this case built on Gemini, and asked: what happens if we treat driving itself as a language problem? So instead of building a specialized architecture with custom heads for detection, prediction, and planning, we feed in the raw camera images along with some text, like a high-level navigation instruction ("turn left at the next intersection") and the ego vehicle's recent history. Then we ask the model to produce the future trajectory directly as text.

Concretely, the trajectory is just a sequence of waypoints, x-y coordinates in the vehicle's frame, written out as plain-text numbers. There's no special tokenization trick and no regression head. The model "speaks" the trajectory the same way it would answer a question. That sounds almost naive, but it works quite well, because these models have absorbed a great deal of world knowledge and spatial reasoning from pretraining, and expressing outputs in language lets you tap into that directly.

What I find most compelling is that once everything is text, you can unify many tasks in one model. The same model that outputs the planned trajectory can also output 3D object detections or road graph elements, again just as text, and you can co-train on all of them. We saw that this co-training actually helps: learning to detect objects and understand road structure improves planning quality. You can also prompt the model to do chain-of-thought reasoning before it commits to a trajectory. It might first describe the critical objects in the scene, explain what they're likely to do, and state a meta-decision like "yield to the pedestrian." Then it outputs the waypoints. That improved performance, and it also gives you some interpretability into why the model chose what it did.

We got strong results on public benchmarks like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, competitive with or better than more specialized approaches.

That said, I want to be clear about what this is and isn't. EMMA is a research exploration, not our production stack. It has real limitations. It's camera-only, so it doesn't use lidar or radar, which matter a lot for robust 3D understanding and safety. It processes a limited number of frames, so long temporal context is a challenge. And these large models are computationally expensive, which is a serious constraint when you need to run in real time on a vehicle. There's also the question of how you validate and verify a system like this to the standard autonomous driving requires.

So the way I think about it is that EMMA is a really useful signal about where the field can go. Foundation models bring generalization and world knowledge that are very valuable, especially for the long tail of unusual situations. The open question is how to combine that power with the precision, efficiency, and safety guarantees you need on the road. My view is that the answer will likely be some hybrid, where these large models inform and complement more structured, rigorously validated components rather than replacing everything outright.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things that I think is actually quite elegant about EMMA, and it's a departure from how we've traditionally built these systems. The classical autonomous driving stack is modular. You have perception that produces boxes and tracks, you have a prediction module that forecasts where other agents will go, you have a planner that consumes all of that and produces a trajectory. Each of those has its own representation, its own interface, and a lot of engineering goes into those interfaces.

With EMMA, we asked a different question, which is: what if the trajectory is just language? What if the output of the model is literally text? So the way it works is we take the camera images, we take the routing information, the high-level navigation command, maybe some ego history, and we feed that into a Gemini-based multimodal model. And then we ask it to produce the future trajectory as a sequence of waypoints, and those waypoints are expressed as text tokens, as numbers in the model's natural output vocabulary.

Now, the first reaction many people have is, that seems a little strange, why would you represent continuous driving behavior as text? And I think the answer is that it lets you inherit everything the foundation model already knows. The model has seen an enormous amount of the world, it understands what a cyclist is, it understands that an ambulance with lights on means something different than a parked car, and it can reason about those things in a way that a narrow, task-specific network trained only on driving logs really struggles with. By keeping everything in the language space, you don't have to design special heads or special decoders to bolt the driving task onto the model. You just ask it.

The second thing that becomes very natural is chain-of-thought. Because the output is language, you can have the model talk through its reasoning before it commits to a trajectory. It can say, there's a pedestrian on the right who looks like they're about to cross, there's a vehicle stopped ahead, the light is green, therefore I'm going to slow and yield. And then the waypoints follow from that. We found that actually improves the quality of the trajectories, not just the interpretability, and I think that's a very interesting signal about where this is going.

The third thing is co-training. Because the format is unified, we can train the same model on 3D object detection, on road graph estimation, on scene understanding, all as text, alongside the trajectory prediction. And those tasks help each other. That's something that's much harder to do in a modular stack where each component has its own loss and its own representation.

Now, I want to be careful here. EMMA is a research model. It's not what's driving the cars today. There are real limitations. It's operating on camera only, it has limited temporal context, it's expensive to run at the latencies a vehicle needs, and we haven't yet integrated lidar and radar into it. The trajectory is also an open-loop prediction, so you have to be very thoughtful about how you'd actually close the loop and validate that in a safety-critical setting. But as an existence proof that a large multimodal model can do end-to-end driving competitively on our benchmarks, and do it with reasoning and generalization that the classical stack doesn't give you for free, I think it's a pretty important result, and it informs how we think about the next generation of the Waymo Driver.

astra-6.text:
I think of the trajectory as another output modality. A vision-language model takes in images and text and generates tokens, and you can represent a future driving trajectory as a sequence of tokens as well. So instead of asking it to describe the scene, you’re asking, “Given what you see, and given where you’re trying to go, how should the vehicle move?”

What’s interesting is that this brings driving into the same framework as other tasks. You can ask the model to describe what’s happening, identify something relevant to the driving decision, or predict a trajectory. Those tasks can potentially reinforce one another.

But producing a plausible trajectory is only part of the problem. Driving is a closed-loop task: you execute some of that motion, get new observations, and make another decision. So the important question is how well those predictions translate into reliable behavior as the situation evolves.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about it is that the trajectory is another modality the model can express. A language model normally produces a sequence of tokens representing words. Here, we train it to produce a sequence that represents the vehicle’s future motion, conditioned on the visual input and the driving instruction.

That lets us bring perception, prediction, and planning into a common framework. But generating a plausible trajectory is only part of the problem. For driving, you need to understand whether that trajectory is safe, how it interacts with other road users, and how reliably the system behaves in unusual situations. So I think of this as a promising way to explore end-to-end driving, with substantial work still needed to evaluate and validate that capability.
